nameStory: The marsh grass shrimp gets its name from its favorite hangout spots — the grassy edges of salt marshes and tidal creeks where marsh grasses sway in the current. These little crustaceans love to dart between the stems and blades, using the grass as both shelter and hunting grounds. The 'grass' part of their name also hints at their see-through, almost grass-green appearance that helps them blend in perfectly.
description: Marsh grass shrimp are tiny, nearly transparent crustaceans that look like miniature versions of the shrimp on your dinner plate. These little guys grow to less than 2 inches long and have the classic shrimp shape with long antennae, curved bodies, and fan-like tails. Their bodies are so clear you can almost see through them, except for distinctive orange-colored eyestalks that look like tiny traffic cones. They're one of the most common small shrimp species along our New England coast.

idTips.label: Orange eyestalks
idTips.description: Look for bright orange patches on the eyestalks that stand out like little beacons against the otherwise clear body — this is the most reliable field mark

idTips.label: Transparent body
idTips.description: The body is so clear it's almost like looking at a glass sculpture of a shrimp — you can often see internal organs and food moving through the digestive tract

idTips.label: Small size
idTips.description: Adults reach less than 2 inches long, about the size of your thumbnail, making them much smaller than commercial shrimp

idTips.label: Swimming motion
idTips.description: They dart backward with quick flicks of their fan-shaped tail when startled, making sudden jerky movements through the water

idTips.label: Long antennae
idTips.description: Two pairs of long, thread-like antennae that are often longer than the body itself and constantly wave around sensing the environment

habitat: You'll find marsh grass shrimp in shallow, brackish waters along New England's coast, especially in salt marshes, tidal pools, and the grassy edges of estuaries. They love areas where saltwater mixes with fresh water and plenty of marsh grasses like cordgrass provide cover. Look for them in water that's usually less than a few feet deep, often darting around submerged vegetation or hiding in the shadows of docks and piers.

seasonality.spring: Shrimp become more active as waters warm, with young juveniles appearing in shallow areas. This is when you'll start seeing them in tidal pools and marsh edges again.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity season when they're most abundant and easiest to spot. Adults are actively feeding and reproducing, making them more visible in shallow waters.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to move to slightly deeper waters. Numbers may seem lower as they start their seasonal migration patterns.
seasonality.winter: Least active period when they retreat to deeper, warmer waters and are rarely seen in shallow tidal areas.

funFact: Marsh grass shrimp are living mood rings — they can actually change their color and transparency based on their surroundings and the time of day, becoming more opaque at night and nearly invisible during bright daylight to avoid predators!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other small grass shrimp species, but those orange eyestalks are your best friend — no other common grass shrimp in New England has such distinctly colored eye patches. Remember: 'Orange eyes, marsh grass prize!'
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the name 'common American prawn' confuse you — in America, we typically call these creatures shrimp, while 'prawn' is more of a British term. They're the same type of animal, just different names on different sides of the Atlantic!
compareHints: Among its glass shrimp relatives, the marsh grass shrimp is the only one with those distinctive orange eyestalks — the Eastern grass shrimp lacks this coloration, while the Daggerblade grass shrimp has different body proportions. The Oriental shrimp is an introduced species that's typically found in more urban harbor areas rather than natural marsh habitats.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Rockpool prawns can be distinguished from other Palaemon glass shrimp in New England by their habitat preference for rocky tide pools rather than salt marshes or estuaries.
Oriental Shrimp can be distinguished from other Palaemon species by their exceptionally long antennae and more pronounced rostrum.
Eastern Grass Shrimp are distinguished from their close relatives like Daggerblade Grass Shrimp by their freshwater habitat preference, while Daggerblade species prefer brackish or saltwater marshes.

Among its glass shrimp relatives, the daggerblade stands out with its distinctive brownish spots scattered across the transparent body - other Palaemon species in New England waters tend to be more uniformly colored or have different spot patterns.
Compared to the more common Marsh Grass Shrimp and Eastern Grass Shrimp in New England waters, Palaemon mundusnovus is distinguished by subtle differences in antenna proportions and body shape.
